extracted.intended_audience: general public; aspiring improvisers, theater students, and people curious about improv
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and core principles for creating and performing improvised (short-form and long-form) theatrical scenes, including games, rules, and collaborative habits that produce strong improv. Covers both practical techniques (games, prompts, roles) and interpersonal practices (listening, 'yes, and').

rubrics_metrics.name: Unscripted creation / live invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv is a live performance in which the actors make up scenes, dialogue and characters on the spot (sometimes incorporating suggestions from the audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everything from what the performers say to the faces they make to how they move their bodies is entirely made up on the spot. Emphasizes the absence of prewritten dialog and reliance on spontaneous choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form vs long-form structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When improvisers use prompts within scenes or games lasting a few minutes, it’s called 'short-form' improv. In 'long-form' improv, performers develop a lengthier scene, similar to a short play, based on a single premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-form favors many quick games/scenes often with audience prompts; long-form focuses on deeper development from one premise and sustained narrative. Both formats are commonly presented together in shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporating audience suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvised scenes often incorporate suggestions from the audience (e.g., a location or an occupation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers solicit and use audience-provided locations, occupations, or other prompts as seeds for scenes; this practice helps ground scenes and creates audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of theater games (Viola Spolin methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv training and exercises often derive from Viola Spolin’s theater games, which are designed to develop improvisational skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games like Contact and Gibberish teach rules-based play and ensemble skills. Spolin’s games are used for training actors and for structuring short-form activities; many modern improv conventions trace directly to her 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of Concentration / goal-focused play
rubrics_metrics.description: Each game should have a 'Point of Concentration,' or a goal the players are trying to achieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on a specific problem or goal gets performers out of their own heads and into the scene, enabling problem-solving that produces spontaneity. The guidance emphasizes that constraint + group decision creates energy and freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Yes, and' — never deny an offered reality
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Yes, and' (synthesis of Spolin’s philosophy): never deny someone’s reality; accept offers and build on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene partner establishes a reality (e.g., 'I'm a talking hedgehog'), you should not negate it (e.g., 'no, actually you are a car'); instead accept and add information (e.g., ask to use the quill). 'Yes, and' is also summarized as active listening and generous collaboration and has applications beyond theater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make active choices (rather than passive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer making active rather than passive choices in a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active choices move the scene forward and shape dynamics; this precept was part of the 'Kitchen Rules' referenced by practitioners like Del Close and colleagues. Active decisions help create clarity and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listening, presence, and generosity to scene partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong improvisers listen, care, and give scene partners 'gifts'—they are present and collaborative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improv requires close listening and attention; being 'really present working with a group' aids scene development. Good improvised work is as much interpersonal skill as comedic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of constraints and rules to generate spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of games and group-bound constraints generate the energy and spontaneity central to improv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spolin: 'The energy released to solve the problem, being restricted by the rules of the game and bound by group decision, creates an explosion or spontaneity.' Constraints focus action and enable expressive freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv as a method for creating sketch material
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation can be used to develop written sketches and prewritten comedy; sketch comedy and improv are distinct but related practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches are often prewritten or hybrid; shows like SNL are sketch-based but may use improv during development. Many improv-trained performers develop material that later becomes scripted.
